y1-early.name: Beyond Antiquity: Art and Architecture until 1750
y1-early.content:
This course provides a comprehensive overview of the development of the visual arts and architecture in Europe from Antiquity to the Early Modern period, focusing on the artistic, technical, and intellectual transformations that defined these eras. It examines how the arts
evolved under the influence of the Church, theological teachings, and new materials. It explores how stylistic and iconographic changes in art can be explained and considers the role of not only theological but also secular factors, such as the ambitions of city councils or noble families. In addition to sacred art (e.g., church painting, sculpture, manuscripts), the emergence of distinct secular architecture in the late Middle Ages is also addressed.
Furthermore, it focuses on the radical innovations of the Renaissance, the definition of art and the artist, the imitation of nature, and the emergence of new formats and genres (e.g., portrait painting, landscape depictions, printmaking). In architecture, the course covers the
Renaissance in Florence, the development of Baroque and Rococo styles, and the interplay between architecture and cultural movements. The methodology includes the analysis of artworks and buildings using visual materials, floor plans, and historical sources, as well as discussions of primary sources and secondary literature. The application of specialized terminology for describing and classifying styles, techniques, and functions is emphasized.

y1-gardens.name: Gardens and Parks: The Green Heritage of Europe
y1-gardens.content:
The course offers a concise overview of the development of European gardens and parks, their design and cultural history from antiquity till the 20th century. This course reflects the interdisciplinary approach to garden history. To understand the significance of gardens, you need to take some notion of horticulture, botany, archaeology, aesthetics, art, sociology, anthropology, technic, politics, food and much else.
The development of the European garden will be examined through iconic examples, providing students with insight into the main gardens, parks, and trends of the period. In the seminars, students learn to analyse the architecture and spatial characteristics. The focus will be on style, function and cultural representation.  In addition, the seminars develop skills such as understanding the drawing traditions of landscape design and the use of garden terminology.

y1-methods.name: Paint, Plaster, Plant: How To Do Art History
y1-methods.content:
Throughout all ages and in all cultures, artworks are at once representational and material, transcendent image and physical stuff. It is this particular form of being material and representational at once that allows artworks to tell stories, evoke associations, and send messages to a viewer. Materials and techniques determine form, style and aesthetics and artists chose them intentionally to convey ideas and create effects. If we want to understand what art means, we need to study its materials, techniques, and representations side by side. 

The field of art history has developed different approaches to doing so and the aim of this course is to teach students how to look at, analyse, and engage critically and confidently with its diverse objects. It serves as an introduction for art history students to the basic tools they need for thinking about, interpreting, and starting to write about works of art and architecture. These include, but are not limited to, formalism, iconography, social history, material studies, technical art history, and other object-based approaches, including primary sources, materials, and techniques. During the seminar, students will learn how to engage hands-on with art and architecture in order to experience and learn what art can tell them about the visual and material world all around them.

The course is trans-chronological and cross-cultural in scope.

y1-ecologies.name: Into the Fields: Ecologies of Art, Architecture and Landscape
y1-ecologies.content: How do the disciplines of art, architecture and landscape contribute and respond to today’s environmental issues? This course introduces students to in-depth archival research and field research, where the strict separations between disciplines dissipates. By focussing on concepts of sustainability, circularity and regeneration, we learn how our object-based approaches make these disciplines both materially grounded and conceptually expansive.

y1-impact.name: Cultural Heritage: Classical Worlds and the Making of Heritage
y1-impact.entry:
This module is open for:
* students of the BA Archaeology
* students of the BA Art History
* students of the BA Arts, Culture and Media
* students of the BA Classical Studies
* students of the BA History
* students of the BA Middle Eastern Studies
* exchange students at the Faculty of Arts
y1-impact.content:
In this course, you study the past from the perspectives of different disciplines and explore the lasting influence of cultural heritage on understandings of the past today. 
The primary focus is on the prominence of classical Greece and Rome across the globe, in architecture, the arts, politics, and literature. You will explore how the notion of heritage developed around Greco-Roman intellectual and artistic paradigms, and how classical antiquity has been ideologically and politically appropriated in modern historical contexts. You will consider how disciplinary frameworks such as archaeology, classics, art history, history, literary studies, political science, and theatre studies have shaped understandings of the classical past. In addition, you will critically interrogate the privileged position of Greece and Rome within Western traditions. You will engage with the interdisciplinary perspectives of classical reception studies and Critical Ancient World Studies that contribute to reshaping contemporary conceptions of heritage.

y1-modern-architecture.name: Modern to Contemporary: Architecture 1750-now
y1-modern-architecture.content:
Modern to Contemporary: Architecture provides an overview of architectural history since 1750 until now. The course is developed chronologically and thematically and explores Revivalism and Eclecticism, Beaux-Arts, Belle Epoque and Art Nouveau, and Art Deco, as well as pre-war and interwar modernism, International Style, Socialist Realism, and the architecture of post-colonial spaces, postmodernism, and the contemporary architecture in general terms. This class examines architectural styles and movements, canonical projects, new or existing ideologies, and, most importantly, the dynamics of change and the forces empowering and enforcing it. 

This course uses David Watkin’s A History of Western Architecture and William Curtis’ Modern Architecture Since 1900 as complementary readings. The lectures will provide a learning foundation for the study of architectural history, highlighting socio-political, cultural, and economic trends and the specifics of Western and global architecture since 1750 until today.

y1-modern-art.name: Modern to Contemporary: Art 1750-now
y1-modern-art.content:
This module focuses on developments in the visual arts, beginning in the early 19th century and extending well into the 20th century, a period that spans from the historical avant-garde movements to the latest trends in postmodern art. Against the backdrop of social and political change, increasing industrialization, and technological developments, artistic practices evolved and embraced new forms of expression, styles, materials, technologies, and subjects.
The course traces some of the paths artists have taken and the artistic scenes they were part of, and examines the explosion and parallel succession of movements, from Neoclassicism to Conceptual Art, as well as the emergence of major artistic centers such as Paris and New York. At the same time, it considers how these centers were shaped through broader global networks of exchange, colonial entanglements, migration, and transcultural interaction, and how, over the course of the 20th century, they increasingly shared their prominence with a multiplicity of other artistic contexts and scenes. By addressing the movement of artists, objects, and ideas across borders, the course critically contextualizes established narratives of art history and reconsiders the so-called “canon” from global and postcolonial perspectives.


As part of this course, a museum visit is scheduled; students have to cover their own travel and admission costs.

y2-architecture.name: Architectural (R)evolutions
y2-architecture.entry: Admission by having obtained a (preliminary) positive BSA.
y2-architecture.content: This course examines the key moments in history and their connections to architecture. Focusing on the period from 1750 to the present, we investigate momentous social, economic, and cultural events - such as the construction of the Berlin Wall, the post-colonial built environment, and postwar reconstruction, to name a few - that have shaped architectural production, which in turn has influenced these historical events and processes.

y2-netherlands.name: Art and Architecture of the Netherlands in Global Contexts
y2-netherlands.entry: Admission by having obtained a (preliminary) positive BSA.
y2-netherlands.content:
This Year 2 course examines the art and architecture of the Netherlands from a transnational perspective. Spanning from the early modern period to the twentieth century, the course explores how Dutch artistic and architectural production was shaped by exchanges with other
regions of the world through colonialism, human mobility, and cultural encounters, and, in turn, how the art and architecture of our region changed. Students will investigate, for example, the relationship between art and trade during the Dutch Golden Age, including the circulation of objects, images, and ideas across Asia and the Americas. The course also
considers how global networks influenced urban development, architectural design, and representations of cultural identity within the Netherlands itself. Moving into the modern era, attention shifts to international modernism, global architectural movements, postcolonial
perspectives, and debates surrounding heritage, memory, and preservation. Through case studies, students will develop critical tools to understand the Netherlands not as an isolated national tradition but as part of interconnected global histories. The course encourages
interdisciplinary analysis and reflection on the continuing impact of colonial and global histories on art, architecture, and cultural heritage today.

y2-early-worlds.name: Early Art Worlds: Invention and Exchange in Transcultural Comparison
y2-early-worlds.entry: Admission by having obtained a (preliminary) positive BSA.
y2-early-worlds.content:
This course introduces second-year students to the variously connected and isolated artistic cultures of China, Europe, and the Islamicate world through a comparative and global perspective. Focusing on key case studies, areas, and periods, the course examines how different societies validated indigenous and exotic objects, materials, and visual traditions, as well as how they circulated across regions, cultures, and thought systems. Students will explore a wide range of artistic content, forms, and media while engaging with methods from art history to understand the varying priorities of several cultures for artistic production, material technologies, and workshop practices. 

The course also considers the role of human mobility in shaping artistic encounters and investigates how religion, political power, and social structures informed visual and material culture. Drawing on postcolonial theory and global art-historical approaches, students will critically reflect on how “art worlds” have been constructed, categorized, and interpreted within modern scholarship and museum practices. Through lectures, discussions, and object-based analysis, the course develops skills in visual interpretation, comparative analysis, and critical engagement with sources and histories that continue to expand the remit of art history as well as neighbouring disciplines.

y2-preservation.name: Caring for the Past: History and Theories of Preservation in Art, Architecture and Landscape
y2-preservation.entry: Admission by having obtained a (preliminary) positive BSA.
y2-preservation.content:
As the concept of cultural heritage continues to evolve, revealing new ways in which societies engage with their past, approaches to its care and preservation have also changed. This evolution is reflected in the terminology used to describe such practices, which varies across temporal and geographical contexts as well as between disciplines. The course Caring for the Past focuses on the history and theories developed for the preservation of art, architecture, and landscape heritage.
We will examine preservation in relation to neighbouring concepts such as conservation, restoration, and protection, exploring their meanings, historical development, and contemporary applications. Particular attention will be given to the connections between these practices and the histories of art, architecture, and landscape, as well as to their specificities.
The course also aims to develop knowledge of key institutions involved in art, architectural, and landscape heritage in the Netherlands and internationally, alongside their current perspectives on preservation and care. Finally, it highlights the contemporary relevance of these issues by addressing challenges arising from environmental pressures. Against this general background, the course content may be adapted in accordance with the expertise, research interests, and perspectives of the teaching team.

y2-theory.name: Things and Theories: On Concepts, Objects, and Interpretation
y2-theory.entry: Admission by having obtained a (preliminary) positive BSA.
y2-theory.content:
This class explores core theoretical concepts from art history, architectural history, and the history of landscape. Ranging from formal analysis to feminist, post-colonial, political, and (new-)materialist theories, it provides a historiographical introduction to the emergence and relevance of theory for the object-based fields, offers insights into the main characteristics and objectives of different theories, and outlines their limitations, biases, and blind spots.

During the course, students will also learn the difference between theories and methods/methodologies, practice applying different theoretical models, and develop a theoretical framework for a potential research project.

y2-exhibition.name: From Studio to Exhibition: Practices and Publics in Contemporary Art
y2-exhibition.entry: Admission by having obtained a (preliminary) positive BSA.
y2-exhibition.content: From Studio to Exhibition: Practices and Publics in Contemporary Art offers a survey of contemporary art from the 1990s to the present. The history of contemporary art contains a tapestry of stories. Rather than following a strict chronological, geographical, or stylistic line, the course is structured by recurring and often debated topics revolving around Memory, Identity, Placement, Digitization. Attention will be paid to the institutional, social and political contexts in which contemporary art developed, as well as to developments in the infrastructure and functioning of Art Worlds. By studying the biography of artworks, we will explore life cycles and trajectories of works of art, from studio to exhibition and beyond. The course provides tools to critically analyze and reflect on the art (world) of today.

y2-landscapes.name: Real and Imagined Landscapes
y2-landscapes.entry: Admission by having obtained a (preliminary) positive BSA.
y2-landscapes.content:
This course takes the real, as in the physical landscape, as an anchor to explore histories of designed landscapes and question how we imagine the future. We study how the development of these landscapes is both pragmatically and creatively formed. Culture not only reflects but also informs how land is used, shaped and experienced. Therefore we also consider how artists engage with themes like climate change and the loss of biodiversity. Through field research, artists and architects talks, and hands-on assignments we strive to create a lively and motivating learning environment. 

Please be aware that for this course you will have to spend 60 euros on mandatory excursions (bus trip, museum or garden visit, and artist talk).

y2-impact.name: Cultural Heritage: Heritage in a Changing World
y2-impact.entry:
This module is open for: 
- students with a positive BSA from all BA programmes at the Faculty of Arts (*)
(*) The following BA programmes do not take part in 2026-2027:
Dutch Languages and Cultures; History; Linguistics.
y2-impact.content:
The course introduces the concept of heritage, charts its intellectual and material histories, and addresses the complex challenges that cultural heritage faces in a rapidly changing global context: affected by climate change and political crisis, responding to decolonization, restitution, and identity formation; negotiating values between material authenticity and digital copies, depending on volatile infrastructures and institutions, and balancing environmental footprint and handprint, heritage is under pressure to survive in and beyond the 21st Century.

Weekly lectures address these and other crucial themes in heritage discourses, including practical aspects such as methods to analyse and care for heritage and state-of-the-art information about heritage institutions and heritage management. Each lecture unfolds the topic of the week, building on relevant publications and highlighting the interdisciplinarity of the field. Each lecture uses at least two case studies, including wherever possible, one from a non-western context and one from the Netherlands. The course introduces students interested in a career in the heritage sector to basic theoretical and practical aspects.

y3-practice.name: Practice Lab: Art/Architecture/Landscape
y3-practice.entry: To participate in this course, the first year of the degree programme must be successfully completed.
y3-practice.content:
In your final months as students in the Bachelor in Art History, we challenge you to apply (elements of) what you have learnt so far to real life situations. In this course you analyse and reflect upon actual projects in the cultural field. These projects typically combine aspects of visual art, architecture, and landscape and are in need of expertise with regard to for instance:
-	the historical background of artefacts, landscapes and built structures
-	ecological, political, social & conservation issues
-	contested heritage
-	cultural and economic impact, interests of different stakeholders

y3-excursion.name: Excursion Art & Architecture
y3-excursion.entry:
To participate in this excursion, the first year of the degree programme must be successfully completed. 
Only for students of the Art History program.
y3-excursion.content:
This academic year, two excursion destinations are offered: Berlin and Florence (note - the latter has a limited number of participants). Students sign up for one of the destinations with an argued preference. If selection is needed, it will be performed by the lecturers.

As for the first, an excursion to Berlin, Germany is offered. Berlin houses many artists, architects, galleries, private and public museums, with diverse collections of first-class art works and more experimental ones, buildings and housing estates that revolutionized architecture and urbanism. Already in the nineteenth century, it was the first city to foster an interconnected museum infrastructure, which until today is being reinterpreted and expanded. Through various (individual and group) assignments, prepared in the weeks prior to departure, and continued and presented in Berlin, students get to know this metropolitan city. With a focus on the period 1800-now, you will practice the visual, material, technological and institutional/museological analysis of artworks and/or focus on major architectural interventions in a historically-defined urban context. We will visit the city, its neighborhoods, architectural sites, major art museums, galleries, artists-led spaces and explore the city’s vibrant art scene. Where possible, meetings with artists, architects, curators and/or gallery staff will take place to provide students with an insider’s view. After the excursion, students present their findings in a paper and project-document.

As for the second, an excursion to Florence, Italy is offered. The city and its works of art, predominantly from the period 1300-1600, will be studied and analyzed 'in situ' from various points: how should we understand them within the historical context in which they originated? How were they seen and 'handled' in later ages? How should they be handled and preserved now and in the future, especially in a city overrun by tourists? An important question will be: How is our present view of Florence shaped by changes and additions from previous centuries? At the end of the excursion, the students will present their findings in a paper.

y3-thesis.name: Bachelor’s Thesis Art History
y3-thesis.entry: The BA thesis may only be started once the first year of the degree programme is successfully completed.
y3-thesis.content: The Bachelor’s thesis is the concluding element of the Bachelor’s degree programme in Art History. The Bachelor’s thesis should be a sound, critical study on a topic chosen by the student in consultation with the supervising lecturer. Students will gain experience in analysing knowledge and insights from the analysis of the objects, buildings or landscapes they study and the literature about it, and learn to critically reflect on and synthesize these insights and identify possible gaps and unanswered questions.

progression: All first-year requirements total 60 EC, with 30 EC each semester. Completing the year meets the 45 EC positive study advice threshold and the named entry condition for major third-year courses.

Year two has 50 EC of compulsory courses and one 10 EC Faculty-Wide Course. The dated catalogue lists Heritage in a Changing World first among the available faculty-wide courses. It accepts Art History students with positive study advice. Selection is independent of UCR fit.

The 30 EC minor is scheduled in the first semester of year three. Practice Lab is in the second semester first block, and the selected Art and Architecture excursion is in its second block. The 15 EC thesis is available in the second semester, counted once, with first-year completion required. The excursion is first in the Part B list; the destination depends on placement and is left open.
